facts.statement: Simosuchus lived during the Late Cretaceous period on the island of Madagascar.
facts.quote: Simosuchus is an extinct genus of notosuchian crocodyliforms from the Late Cretaceous of Madagascar.

facts.statement: The type species Simosuchus clarki was discovered in the Maevarano Formation within Mahajanga Province.
facts.quote: The type species is Simosuchus clarki, found from the Maevarano Formation in Mahajanga Province

facts.statement: An isolated tooth of Simosuchus was found in the Kallamedu Formation in India.
facts.quote: although one isolated multicuspid tooth of this genus was discovered in Kallamedu Formation of India.

facts.statement: Simosuchus was first described in 2000 based on a single initial specimen.
facts.quote: The first specimen of Simosuchus clarki, which served as the basis for its initial description in 2000

facts.statement: Most Simosuchus fossils were recovered by the Mahajanga Basin Project, a collaboration between the Université d'Antananarivo and Stony Brook University.
facts.quote: Most remains of Simosuchus were found as part of the Mahajanga Basin Project, directed by the Université d'Antananarivo and Stony Brook University.

facts.statement: Adult Simosuchus measured approximately 0.75 meters in length.
facts.quote: Fully grown individuals were about 0.75 m in length.

facts.statement: The name Simosuchus refers to the animal's unusually short skull.
facts.quote: It is named for its unusually short skull.

facts.statement: Simosuchus possessed maple-leaf-shaped teeth and a short, deep snout, features distinct from typical carnivorous crocodylomorphs.
facts.quote: The teeth of S. clarki were shaped like maple leaves, which coupled with its short and deep snout suggests it was not a carnivore like most other crocodylomorphs.

facts.statement: Many paleontologists classify Simosuchus as a herbivore based on its dental and cranial morphology.
facts.quote: In fact, these features have led many palaeontologists to consider it a herbivore.

facts.statement: The genus name Simosuchus translates to "pug-nosed crocodile" because its snout resembles that of a pug.
facts.quote: The snout resembles that of a pug, giving the genus its name, which means "pug-nosed crocodile" in Greek.

facts.statement: The skull of Simosuchus contains 45 autapomorphies, or unique features not found in other species.
facts.quote: 45 autapomorphies, or features unique to Simosuchus, can be found in the skull alone.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Simosuchus held its head with the preorbital area angled approximately 45 degrees from the horizontal.
facts.quote: Simosuchus likely held its head so that the preorbital area was angled about 45° from horizontal.

facts.statement: Simosuchus had a broad, three-pronged scapula.
facts.quote: The scapula is broad and tripartite (three-pronged).

facts.statement: Simosuchus possessed robust limbs adapted for terrestrial movement.
facts.quote: The limbs are robust.

facts.statement: Simosuchus featured a tetraserial paravertebral shield composed of four rows of tightly locking paramedial osteoderms along its back.
facts.quote: Simosuchus has a tetraserial paravertebral shield over its back, meaning that there are four rows of tightly locking paramedial osteoderms (osteoderms to either side of the midline of the back).

facts.statement: Simosuchus was fully terrestrial, and its short tail suggests it was not adapted for swimming.
facts.quote: Like other notosuchians, it was fully terrestrial, and the short tail would have had little use in swimming.

facts.statement: The inflexible osteoderm shield of Simosuchus likely restricted lateral movement as an adaptation to a terrestrial lifestyle.
facts.quote: The osteoderm shield was inflexible, restricting lateral movement in Simosuchus as a possible adaptation to an entirely terrestrial lifestyle.

facts.statement: Unlike most other notosuchians, Simosuchus had semierect hindlimbs rather than a fully erect posture.
facts.quote: The hindlimbs of Simosuchus were semierect, unlike the fully erect posture of most other notosuchians.

facts.statement: Simosuchus was initially classified as a basal member of the clade Notosuchia.
facts.quote: Simosuchus was first considered to be a basal member of the clade Notosuchia

facts.statement: In its 2000 description, Simosuchus was placed in the family Notosuchidae.
facts.quote: In its initial description by Buckley et al. (2000), Simosuchus was placed in the family Notosuchidae.

facts.statement: A 2004 study by Carvalho et al. proposed a different phylogenetic relationship for Simosuchus compared to earlier research.
facts.quote: Carvalho et al. (2004), based on different character values than previous studies, produced a very different relationship among Simosuchus and other notosuchians.

facts.statement: Some analyses placed Simosuchus outside the clade Notosuchia alongside Uruguaysuchus and Comahuesuchus.
facts.quote: Simosuchus, along with Uruguaysuchus and Comahuesuchus, were placed outside Notosuchia.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Simosuchus belongs within Notosuchia or is the sister taxon of the Chinese genus Chimaerasuchus in the family Chimaerasuchidae.
facts.quote: Simosuchus was found to be the sister taxon of the Chinese genus Chimaerasuchus in the family Chimaerasuchidae.

facts.statement: Simosuchus had small front feet with large claws and reduced back feet.
facts.quote: The front feet are small with large claws, and the back feet are also reduced in size.

facts.statement: Researchers initially suggested Simosuchus was a burrowing animal based on its robust limbs and short, shovel-like snout.
facts.quote: A fossorial, or burrowing, lifestyle for Simosuchus has been suggested in its initial description based on the robust limbs and short snout, which appears shovel-like

facts.statement: In 2010, Kley and colleagues argued against the burrowing hypothesis, stating the animal's morphology did not show adaptations for head-first burrowing.
facts.quote: In 2010, Kley and colleagues have argued against this hypothesis on the basis of its morphology which doesn't show an adaptation as head-first burrowers
